Pages behind a sign-in must be scanned, which needs a custom scan with a test account, because managed scans do not authenticate.
traps: A scan of production with an admin account. The scanner clicks buttons and submits forms, so scan a test environment with a test account.
Web Security Scanner for an internal-only app. It scans only public IPv4 URLs that are not behind a firewall.

confused.tell: Artifact Analysis finds CVEs in the packages of container images. Web Security Scanner tests the running app.
Security Command Center shows the Web Security Scanner findings together with the findings of many other services.

services.name: Security Command Center
services.what: Security Command Center is a risk management service. It collects findings from its built-in services, from integrated Google Cloud services, and from third-party tools.
cues: Findings from many services must be seen and prioritized in one place.
A vulnerable image runs on Cloud Run, GKE, or App Engine, and the finding must resolve after the fix.
Findings for an isolated test asset do not apply, which fits a mute rule.
traps: A fixed image deployed with --no-traffic. The finding resolves only when no traffic goes to the vulnerable revision.
Muting a finding as the fix. Muting only hides it.

confused.tell: Artifact Analysis scans the images in Artifact Registry. Security Command Center shows image findings only for HIGH and CRITICAL vulnerabilities in deployed images.

services.aws: Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, AWS Config

services.name: Organization Policy Service
services.what: The Organization Policy Service controls which configurations are allowed on resources, and descendant resources inherit each policy. IAM controls who can act on a resource.
cues: No project may make a bucket public or create service account keys, also when IAM allows it.
Resources may be created only in approved locations, which fits the gcp.resourceLocations constraint.
A new constraint must be tested before it denies requests, which fits dry-run mode.
traps: A new organization policy to fix existing resources. Most constraints apply only to new create and update requests.
A service account key exception for a pipeline. New organizations block key creation by default, so use attached service accounts or Workload Identity Federation.

confused.tell: IAM controls who can act on a resource. An organization policy controls which configurations are allowed.

services.name: VPC Service Controls
services.what: VPC Service Controls puts a perimeter around Google Cloud services, such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery, to reduce the risk of data exfiltration. It is independent of IAM, and Google recommends both.
cues: Data in Cloud Storage or BigQuery must not leave a perimeter through Google Cloud APIs.
A Cloud Run service with internal ingress must still receive requests from Pub/Sub, Eventarc, or Cloud Scheduler in the same perimeter.
A deploy from source must build inside a perimeter, which needs a Cloud Build private pool.
traps: VPC Service Controls instead of IAM. Use both.
A Pub/Sub push subscription to a custom domain inside a perimeter. A new push subscription can only target a run.app URL or a Workflows execution.

confused.tell: IAM controls who can call an API. A VPC Service Controls perimeter controls whether data can leave the perimeter through Google Cloud APIs.

services.name: IAM (roles, conditions, and recommendations)
services.what: IAM grants roles to principals on resources. Predefined roles fit most tasks, custom roles fill the gaps, and IAM Conditions limit a grant by time or resource name.
cues: A service must publish to one topic, which fits the Pub/Sub Publisher role on that topic, not on the project.
A contractor needs access to one bucket prefix for 14 days, which fits a predefined role with an IAM condition.
An Editor role must be replaced without breaking the workloads, which fits role recommendations and Policy Simulator.
traps: A condition on an Editor grant. Legacy basic roles do not accept conditions.
A custom role on a folder. Custom roles exist only at the organization or project level.

confused.tell: An organization policy controls which configurations are allowed. IAM controls who can act on a resource.
A service account is an identity for code. IAM roles decide what it can do, and roles on the service account decide who can attach or impersonate it.

services.name: Service accounts and impersonation
services.what: A service account is the identity of a workload, and it is also a resource that other principals get roles on. Code on Google Cloud gets the credentials of its attached service account from the metadata server.
cues: Each Cloud Run service needs its own identity with only the roles that it uses, instead of the Compute Engine default service account.
A deployer must attach a service account to a Cloud Run service, which needs Service Account User on that account.
A developer must test with the permissions of a production workload without a key, which fits impersonation with Service Account Token Creator.
traps: Service Account User for --impersonate-service-account. Impersonation needs Service Account Token Creator, also for a project Owner.
A key file in GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS on Cloud Run or GKE. It overrides the attached service account and Workload Identity Federation for GKE.

confused.tell: Code outside Google Cloud has no attached service account. Workload Identity Federation gives it short-lived credentials with no key.
A service account is the identity. Application Default Credentials is how the client libraries find its credentials.

services.aws: AWS STS AssumeRole, EC2 instance profiles

docs.title: Best practices for using service accounts securely

services.name: Workload Identity Federation
services.what: Workload Identity Federation gives workloads on AWS, on Azure, on premises, or in deployment pipelines access to Google Cloud without a service account key. Workload Identity Federation for GKE is the recommended way for GKE workloads to access Google Cloud services.
cues: A GitHub Actions workflow must deploy to Cloud Run, and an organization policy blocks service account keys.
An app on AWS or Azure must call Google Cloud APIs without a stored key.
Each app in a GKE cluster must call Google Cloud APIs with its own identity and no key file.
traps: A GitHub provider without an attribute condition. GitHub uses one issuer for all organizations, so add a condition for your organization, preferably on its numeric ID.
An untrusted GKE cluster in the same project. All clusters in a project share one workload identity pool, so the same namespace and ServiceAccount name get the same access.

confused.tell: Code on Google Cloud uses its attached service account. Workload Identity Federation is for code outside Google Cloud and for Kubernetes ServiceAccounts on GKE.
A service account key in a secret store is still a long-lived key. Workload Identity Federation needs no key.

services.aws: AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, IAM roles for service accounts on Amazon EKS

services.name: Identity Platform
services.what: Identity Platform is a customer identity and access management (CIAM) platform. It signs in the end users of your app with email and password, phone, social providers, SAML, or OIDC, and it adds MFA and multi-tenancy.
cues: Customers of a consumer app sign in with email and password or with Google, and the backend must verify their ID tokens.
Business customers must sign in through their own SAML providers, with MFA and a separate set of users for each customer.
An app on Firebase Authentication needs SAML, MFA, tenants, or an SLA, which fits an upgrade with no app change.
traps: IAM authentication on a Cloud Run service for customers. Customers have no IAM permissions, so allow unauthenticated calls and verify the ID token in code.
Trusting the claims of a decoded token. Verify the signature, iss, aud, and exp first, and use sub, not the email address, as the user key.

confused.tell: IAP decides who can reach an app, for employees and partners with IAM roles. Identity Platform signs customers in to your app.
OAuth 2.0 authorization lets your app call Google APIs, such as Drive, with the user's consent. Identity Platform signs users in to your own app.

docs.title: Differences between Identity Platform and Firebase Authentication

services.name: OAuth 2.0 and the Google Auth Platform
services.what: OAuth 2.0 lets your app call Google APIs for a user after the user gives consent. You configure the OAuth clients and the consent screen in the Google Auth Platform.
cues: A web app must read files in the Google Drive of each user, which fits the authorization code flow with user consent.
A nightly job must keep calling a Google API for each user, which needs access_type=offline for a refresh token.
Only users in your organization may authorize the app, which fits the Internal user type.
traps: Refresh tokens that stop working after seven days. The app is External and in Testing status, so publish it to In production status.
User credentials on a server for a job that runs as the app. Use a service account, which needs no OAuth client ID and no user consent.

confused.tell: A service account calls APIs as the app, with no user consent. OAuth 2.0 user authorization calls APIs for one user after consent.
Identity Platform signs users in to your app. OAuth 2.0 authorization gets the user's consent to call Google APIs with their data.

docs.title: Using OAuth 2.0 for Web Server Applications

services.name: Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, AlloyDB Auth Proxy, and Language Connectors
services.what: The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, and the Language Connectors authorize database connections with IAM and encrypt the traffic. They do not create a network path, and they support automatic IAM database authentication.
cues: A client with an ephemeral IP address must connect to a Cloud SQL public IP address without authorized networks.
A Ruby or PHP app, or a tool such as psql, must connect with IAM authorization, which fits the Auth Proxy, because Language Connectors exist only for some languages.
A connection pool must use IAM database authentication without expired tokens, which fits automatic mode in a connector.
Cloud SQL must reject every connection that does not come through a connector, which fits connector enforcement.
traps: The Auth Proxy or a connector to reach a private IP address from a network without VPC access. They do not create a network path.
Only the Cloud SQL Client role for an IAM database login. The login also needs the Cloud SQL Instance User role.

confused.tell: Direct VPC egress gives a Cloud Run service a network path to a private IP address. A connector then authorizes and encrypts the connection on that path.
Cloud SQL is the database. The Auth Proxy and the connectors are ways for clients to connect to it with IAM.

docs.title: About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy

services.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
services.what: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (Agent Platform) serves the Gemini API on Google Cloud, with IAM access control. It has global, regional, and multi-region endpoints, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput.
cues: A production app on Cloud Run must call Gemini with its attached service account and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform User role.
ML processing of customer data must stay in the European Union, which fits the eu multi-region endpoint.
Many prompts need no real-time answer, and cost matters, which fits batch inference at a 50% discount.
Requests on Standard pay-as-you-go fail with 429 errors, which needs exponential backoff and the global endpoint.
traps: The global endpoint for a data residency requirement. You cannot control where it processes a request.
A quota increase as the first fix for 429 errors on Standard pay-as-you-go. The errors show temporary contention for shared capacity.

confused.tell: The Gemini models generate the content. Agent Platform is where your code calls them on Google Cloud, with IAM, endpoints, quotas, and batch jobs.
For data that is already in BigQuery, BigQuery ML trains and runs models with SQL, with no data movement.

services.name: Gemini models and the Gemini API
services.what: The Gemini models generate text and structured output from prompts. With the Google Gen AI SDK, code can ask for JSON that follows a schema, declare functions that the model can ask to call, and ground answers in Google Search or your own data.
cues: The app needs valid JSON with the required fields every time, which fits a response_schema.
The model must use live data from your own API, such as an order status, which fits function calling.
Answers need current public information, which fits Grounding with Google Search.
Many requests start with the same large content, which fits context caching.
traps: Google Search grounding and function calling in one request. The API does not support this combination, so send separate requests.
The application/json MIME type without a schema. It is only a strong hint, so add a response_schema.

confused.tell: Agent Platform serves the Gemini API on Google Cloud, with IAM, endpoints, quotas, and batch jobs. The request settings control what the model returns.
Gemini Code Assist helps developers write code. Your app calls the Gemini API to build its own AI features.

services.name: Cloud Logging and Observability Analytics
services.what: Cloud Logging stores timestamped log entries, and the Logs Explorer finds and filters them. Observability Analytics (formerly Log Analytics) runs SQL queries that aggregate log data and join it with trace data.
cues: A Cloud Run or GKE service must send logs with a severity and fields that you can query, with no agent, which fits JSON lines on stdout and stderr.
A team needs the count of an error for each hour of the past two weeks, which fits a SQL query in Observability Analytics.
Container logs must appear under their request log, which needs the trace ID in the logging.googleapis.com/trace field.
traps: A logging agent for a Cloud Run service. Cloud Run collects stdout and stderr itself.
A query that mixes AND and OR without parentheses. In the Logging query language, OR has a higher precedence than AND.

confused.tell: Cloud Monitoring stores metric time series and alerting policies. A log-based metric turns matching log entries into a metric.
Error Reporting groups the error events in log entries that contain stack traces. Cloud Logging stores all the entries.

docs.title: Analyze logs using Logs Explorer and Observability Analytics

services.name: Cloud Monitoring and Managed Service for Prometheus
services.what: Cloud Monitoring stores metric time series, uptime checks, alerting policies, and SLOs. Managed Service for Prometheus collects Prometheus metrics on GKE, so teams keep their PromQL queries and Grafana dashboards.
cues: An error count or a latency value must come from logs that the app already writes, with no code change, which fits a log-based metric.
Services on GKE already expose Prometheus metrics, and the team does not want to run Prometheus servers.
App metrics from Cloud Run must reach Cloud Monitoring, which fits OpenTelemetry through a collector sidecar with instance-based billing.
traps: A user ID or a request URL as a metric label. Each unique combination of label values creates a time series, so use a small set of values.
A new log-based metric to chart last week's errors. It counts only the entries that arrive after you create it.

confused.tell: Cloud Logging stores the individual log entries. Cloud Monitoring stores metrics, and a log-based metric connects the two.
Cloud Trace shows where one request spends its time. Cloud Monitoring shows how a metric changes over time.

services.name: Cloud Trace
services.what: Cloud Trace stores the spans of each request across services and shows their latency. Cloud Run sends request traces automatically, but your code must propagate the trace context to join the services in one trace.
cues: Some requests are slow, and nobody knows which service or call is slow.
Each user request appears as two separate traces, which needs OpenTelemetry instrumentation that propagates the trace context.
Log entries must link to a span, which needs the trace ID and a 16-character hexadecimal span ID in each entry.
traps: Cloud Trace to link the services. Cloud Trace does not propagate context, so each service must pass it on.
A higher Cloud Run sample rate. You cannot configure it, so add your own instrumentation for more detail.

confused.tell: Cloud Profiler shows which functions use the most CPU or memory. Cloud Trace shows which span of a slow request takes the time.

services.name: Error Reporting
services.what: Error Reporting groups error events from log entries that contain a stack trace, and from its API and client libraries. It sends a notification for a new error and for an error that comes back after you resolve it.
cues: A team must see which exceptions are new and how often they occur.
Error messages without a stack trace must appear as error groups, which needs @type set to the ReportedErrorEvent type.
The log buckets use CMEK, so the code must send errors with the Error Reporting client library.
traps: A stack trace logged at WARNING on Cloud Run. The severity must be not set or at least ERROR.
Muted instead of Resolved for a fixed bug. A muted group records no new events, and a resolved group reopens when the error comes back.

confused.tell: Cloud Logging stores every entry. Error Reporting reads the entries that contain stack traces and groups them by exception type and top frames.
Gemini Cloud Assist can explain an error group and look for probable root causes. Error Reporting groups and counts the errors.

services.name: Cloud Profiler
services.what: Cloud Profiler continuously collects CPU and memory-allocation data from production code with low overhead. You add a language-specific agent library to the application.
cues: A service uses much more CPU or memory under normal load, and the team must find the functions that use the most.
The analysis must use production data, with an overhead that is commonly below 0.5%.
traps: No profiles from a service with a user-created service account. Grant the Cloud Profiler Agent role.
Cloud Trace for high CPU use under normal load. Cloud Trace shows the latency of spans, and Cloud Profiler shows the functions that use the most CPU time.

confused.tell: Cloud Trace shows which service or call in a slow request takes the time. Cloud Profiler shows which functions use the most CPU or memory.
